title: Research, Inc. v. United States
articleTitle: The Jurisprudence of Incremental Innovation: A Comprehensive Analysis of Research, Inc. v. United States and the Evolution of Federal R&D Tax Credit Compliance
court: United States District Court, District of Minnesota
subject: Substantiation of Base Period Research Expenses
summary: Denied a research tax credit refund where the taxpayer could not substantiate qualified research expenses for the statutory base period years.

body.text: The federal research and development (R&D) tax credit, formally known as the Credit for Increasing Research Activities under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41, represents one of the most complex and litigated areas of the United States tax code. Since its inception in 1981, the credit has undergone numerous transformations, evolving from a temporary incentive to a permanent fixture of corporate tax strategy through the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015. At its core, the credit is designed to incentivize domestic innovation by providing a dollar-for-dollar tax offset for companies that increase their investment in qualified research. However, the "incremental" nature of the credit introduces a unique set of evidentiary and documentation challenges, most notably the requirement for consistency between current-year expenditures and historical base-period spending. The 1995 decision in Research, Inc. v. United States stands as a definitive judicial milestone in this regard, establishing rigorous standards for the substantiation of base-period data that continue to dictate IRS audit techniques and taxpayer compliance strategies decades later.
The Statutory Architecture and Incremental Logic of Section 41

To understand the profound implications of Research, Inc. v. United States, one must first navigate the structural logic of the Section 41 credit. Unlike a standard deduction, which merely reduces taxable income, the research credit is specifically calculated to reward growth in research intensity. The credit is generally equal to 20% of a taxpayer’s qualified research expenses (QREs) for the taxable year that exceed a calculated "base amount". This base amount is intended to represent the taxpayer’s typical or historical level of research spending relative to its gross receipts. Consequently, the credit is not a subsidy for all R&D; it is a reward for research activities that exceed a pre-defined threshold.

The determination of this threshold involves two primary methods: the Regular Research Credit (RRC) and the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC). Under the RRC, the base amount is the product of a "fixed-base percentage" and the average annual gross receipts of the taxpayer for the four preceding taxable years. For many established taxpayers, the fixed-base percentage is derived from the ratio of total QREs to total gross receipts during the 1984–1988 period. This historical snapshot, often referred to as the "base period," remains a permanent anchor in the credit calculation, making the preservation of decades-old records a matter of contemporary tax consequence.
The Four-Part Test for Qualified Research

Beyond the mathematical calculation, the underlying activities must satisfy a rigorous four-part test to qualify as "qualified research" under Section 41(d)(1). Every project or "business component" claimed by a taxpayer must meet all four criteria simultaneously:

items: The Section 174 Test: The expenditures must be eligible for treatment as expenses under Section 174, meaning they must be incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense. This requires the existence of technical uncertainty regarding the capability, method, or appropriate design of a business component.

The Technological Information Test: The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, fundamentally relying on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

The Business Component Test: The taxpayer must intend to use the information discovered to develop a new or improved business component, defined as a product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention held for sale, lease, or license.

The Process of Experimentation Test: Substantially all of the activities (generally interpreted as 80% or more) must constitute elements of a process of experimentation, which involves identifying uncertainty, identifying alternatives, and conducting an evaluative process like modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error.

cells: Uncertainty of capability, method, or design.

body.text: The complexity of these requirements necessitates that taxpayers maintain a factual nexus between claimed expenses and specific research projects. This nexus is often the primary point of contention in IRS examinations, where agents scrutinize whether the taxpayer has provided a sufficient "bridge" between the QREs and the qualified activities.
Research, Inc. v. United States: The Judicial Enforcement of Consistency

The case of Research, Inc. v. United States, 95-1 USTC ¶ 50,407 (D. Minn. 1995), centers on a taxpayer’s failure to maintain the historical records necessary to satisfy the "consistency requirement" of Section 41(c)(5)(A). The ruling clarified that the burden of proof rests squarely on the taxpayer to substantiate not only its current spending but also the baseline against which that spending is measured.
Factual Background and the "Special System Projects"

Research, Inc. sought to claim additional R&D tax credits for its fiscal year ending September 20, 1985. As part of its claim, the taxpayer included qualified research expenses associated with "special system projects" in its credit-year computation. These projects involved the design and development of customized technical systems. During the ensuing IRS audit, the taxpayer admitted that it had engaged in the same type of "special system projects" during its base period (under the rolling base period rules in effect at the time).

However, when the IRS requested documentation to verify the research expenses incurred for those base-period projects, Research, Inc. revealed that it had destroyed the relevant records for those years. The taxpayer argued that because it could not quantify the base-period expenses, it should be allowed to include the current-year expenses without a corresponding adjustment to its base. This argument was predicated on the notion that a taxpayer’s inability to produce records should not automatically disqualify a claim if the current-year activities were demonstrably qualified.
The Court's Ruling on the Consistency Rule

The United States District Court for the District of Minnesota rejected the taxpayer’s position, ruling in favor of the government. The court emphasized that the research credit is inherently incremental. Section 41(c)(5)(A) mandates that QREs taken into account in computing the fixed-base percentage must be determined on a basis consistent with the determination of QREs for the credit year.

The court held that the relative increase in qualified research expenses could not be accurately measured without considering the expenses incurred during the base period for the same type of projects included in the credit year. By including "special system projects" in the credit year but failing to account for them in the base year, the taxpayer created a distorted measurement of its R&D growth. Essentially, the taxpayer was trying to claim a credit for a "new" category of research that was actually part of its historical routine. The court concluded that failure to maintain sufficient records to accurately substantiate base-period expenditures is grounds for the disallowance of the entire claim.
Second-Order Implications of Research, Inc.

The implications of the Research, Inc. decision are both profound and enduring. It established that the consistency requirement is a "two-way street." If a taxpayer identifies "new" QREs during an audit or through a study—such as high-level supervision or indirect support costs—they must go back and add those same types of expenses to their base-period calculation. This typically results in an upward adjustment of the fixed-base percentage, which in turn increases the base amount and reduces the overall credit.

This creates a significant documentation hurdle for modern taxpayers. Companies that have existed since the 1980s may find themselves unable to defend a regular research credit claim because they cannot prove what their "special projects" were in 1984. This has led many taxpayers to elect the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC), which uses a three-year lookback period rather than the 1980s base period, thereby mitigating the risk associated with the Research, Inc. precedent.
Documentation Standards and the "Substantially All" Threshold

The legacy of Research, Inc. has been amplified by more recent case law and IRS administrative changes that have significantly raised the bar for what constitutes "contemporaneous documentation." The IRS no longer accepts retrospective estimates or uncorroborated testimony from executives as a substitute for hard data.
The 80% Rule in Practice: Little Sandy Coal

In Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner (2021), the Tax Court further refined the "substantially all" requirement as it pertains to the process of experimentation. The court denied credits for the development of tankers and dry docks because the company could not prove that at least 80% of its activities for each business component followed a structured process of experimentation.

The court's analysis in Little Sandy Coal highlights a critical pitfall: taxpayers often confuse general design challenges with technological uncertainty. To satisfy the IRS, a taxpayer must identify specific uncertainties at the outset of the project—not just general design goals—and document the iterative steps taken to resolve those uncertainties. Failure to identify specific information that was not available to engineers at the start of the project can disqualify the entire claim.
Contemporary Documentation Requirements: Section G and Form 6765

The IRS is currently codifying these judicial standards through administrative changes. Starting in the 2026 tax year, the IRS will mandate the use of Section G on Form 6765. This new section requires taxpayers to document their research on a business-component basis, listing significant components alongside the associated wages for each scientist or engineer.

This change effectively ends the era of "aggregate" R&D claims. Taxpayers must now designate salaries for direct research, direct supervision, and direct support for each individual project. This level of detail is a direct response to the documentation failures seen in Research, Inc. and its successors. By requiring project-level detail at the time of filing, the IRS aims to eliminate the "haphazard method" of retrospective substantiation used by many consultants.
Funded Research and the Smith Case: Defining Economic Risk

Another critical exclusion discussed in modern R&D litigation is "funded research" under Section 41(d)(4)(H). Research is considered funded—and therefore ineligible for the credit—if the taxpayer does not retain "substantial rights" to the research or if the taxpayer is not at "economic risk" for the success of the research.

In Smith v. Commissioner (2024), the Tax Court denied the IRS’s motion for summary judgment, ruling that genuine issues of material fact existed regarding whether architectural design services were "funded". The IRS argued that the firm was paid regardless of the research outcome because it followed professional standards. However, the court found that because the contract tied payment to "design milestones," there was a plausible argument that payment was contingent on the success of the research.

Payment must be contingent on research success.
Executive testimony must be detailed and corroborated.
Basic calculations do not equal research.

body.text: These cases demonstrate that the construction and engineering industries must perform a thorough analysis of contractual terms. Simply performing technical work is not enough; the taxpayer must prove that if the research fails, they—not their client—suffer the financial loss.
Legislative Shifts: Section 174 Amortization and the TCJA

The landscape of R&D tax incentives was further complicated by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) of 2017. Prior to 2022, taxpayers could immediately deduct domestic research and experimental (R&E) expenditures under Section 174. Beginning in 2022, the TCJA required taxpayers to capitalize and amortize these costs over five years for domestic research and 15 years for foreign research.

This shift significantly increased the tax liability for R&D-intensive companies. While the research credit under Section 41 remains available, its utility is inextricably linked to the definition of R&E under Section 174. Furthermore, Section 280C(c) requires that any Section 174 deduction be reduced by the amount of the research credit taken, unless the taxpayer elects to take a reduced credit. Recent legislation, such as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, has permanently restored the immediate expensing of some domestic R&E while maintaining the requirement to "tax-effect" all research credits beginning in 2025.
Strategic Implications for Future R&D Credit Applications
The synthesis of Research, Inc. and modern administrative mandates suggests several critical strategies for taxpayers seeking to claim the R&D credit in the coming years.
The Shrinking-Back Rule as a Defense Mechanism

If a taxpayer cannot meet the four-part test for an entire product, they should apply the "shrinking-back rule". This rule allows the tests to be applied to the most significant subset of elements of a product. This process continues until either a subset satisfies the requirements or the most basic element is reached. By identifying business components at a granular level, taxpayers can protect credits for the truly innovative parts of a project even if the overall project contains non-qualifying elements like commercial production or adaptation.
Enhancing Contemporaneous Substantiation

Taxpayers must move away from retrospective studies and toward real-time documentation systems. The IRS now expects clear documentation of technological uncertainty at the outset of a project. Best practices include:

items: Maintaining a clear breakdown of business components.
Linking every expense directly to a research activity or technical uncertainty.
Recording the "process of experimentation" as it happens, including failed attempts and iterations.

body.text: The economic risk when dealing with the IRS is "greater than meets the eye". For example, a recent case involving Kyocera resulted in costs nearly 10 times the amount of the original credit due to retrospective substantiation issues.
Navigating the Consistency Requirement

For companies using the regular research credit method, a "consistency audit" of the 1984–1988 base period is essential. If the current credit year includes new types of expenses (e.g., software developers or quality assurance engineers) that did not exist or were not claimed in the 1980s, the taxpayer must adjust their fixed-base percentage to reflect those same types of costs during the base years. Failure to perform this analysis—the exact mistake made in Research, Inc.—will likely lead to a disallowance of the credit upon examination.

Conclusion

Research, Inc. v. United States remains a cornerstone of R&D tax credit jurisprudence because it addresses the most fundamental aspect of the credit: its incremental nature. The case serves as a permanent reminder that tax credits are a matter of "legislative grace" and that the burden of substantiating a claim rests entirely with the taxpayer. As the IRS transitions to more automated and granular review systems, such as the Classifier and the Section G requirements of Form 6765, the documentation standards established in 1995 will become even more critical.

The future of the R&D tax credit in the USA will be defined by a shift from "narrative-based" claims to "data-based" claims. Taxpayers who fail to maintain contemporaneous, project-level records that align with the four-part test—and who cannot demonstrate consistency with their historical baseline—will find themselves at significant risk of disallowance and penalties. In the modern era of high-frequency innovation, the most valuable tool in a taxpayer’s arsenal is no longer just their engineering talent, but their ability to document that talent’s work with the precision required by the law.
